title: Medicare Eligibility: Who Qualifies for Medicare Coverage?
summary: Explains who qualifies for Medicare by age, disability or medical condition, how automatic enrollment works, eligibility for each private plan type, citizenship rules, and veterans' benefits.

assets.alt: Are you eligible for Medicare? Medicare eligibility requirements

atoms.title: Who becomes eligible for Medicare
atoms.question: Am I eligible for Medicare?
atoms.text: Most people become eligible for Medicare when they turn 65. You can also become eligible if you have a qualifying disability at any age (eligibility begins after 24 months of receiving Social Security Disability Insurance benefits), or if you have a diagnosis of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, also called Lou Gehrig's disease) at any age.

atoms.title: Automatic versus self-enrollment in Original Medicare
atoms.question: Will I be enrolled in Original Medicare automatically?
atoms.text: You will be enrolled in Original Medicare automatically if you are receiving Social Security or Railroad Retirement Board benefits when you turn 65, or if you are eligible because of a disability or medical condition. You must enroll yourself in Medicare Part A and Part B if you are not receiving Social Security benefits when you become eligible, online at www.ssa.gov, in person at your local Social Security office or by phone at 1-800-772-1213 / TTY 1-800-325-0778.

atoms.title: Age 65 is what matters for eligibility
atoms.question: Will I be eligible for Medicare at age 65?
atoms.text: You are eligible for Medicare when you turn 65, whether you are working, not working or retired, and whether or not you receive Social Security or other retirement benefits. Your age is what matters. If you receive Social Security Disability Insurance payments, you will be eligible for Medicare the month you receive your 25th benefit payment, while ESRD or ALS qualifies you immediately or within a few months depending on your diagnosis.

atoms.title: Eligibility if you work past 65
atoms.question: Will I still be eligible for Medicare if I work past age 65?
atoms.text: Yes. If you plan to keep working or you have employer health coverage through a spouse, you may be able to delay enrolling in Medicare. Depending on your situation you may not be able to delay; for example, if your employer has fewer than 20 employees, you may be required to enroll in Medicare.

atoms.title: Eligibility rules for each private Medicare plan
atoms.question: How do I qualify for a private Medicare plan?
atoms.text: Once you are enrolled in Original Medicare (Part A and Part B), you can choose coverage from a private insurance company. To be eligible for a Medicare Advantage (Part C) plan, you must have Original Medicare and live in the plan service area. A Chronic Special Needs plan (C-SNP) requires Original Medicare and a qualifying chronic condition. A Dual Special Needs plan (D-SNP) requires that you qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid. A Medicare Supplement (Medigap) plan requires Original Medicare. A Part D plan requires Part A or Part B. All Special Needs plans are Medicare Advantage plans.

atoms.title: Citizenship and residency requirements
atoms.question: Do I need to be a U.S. citizen to be eligible for Medicare?
atoms.text: Yes, or a qualified legal resident. To qualify as a legal resident, you must have lived in the United States for at least 5 years in a row before applying for Medicare coverage.

atoms.title: Premium-free Part A if you never worked
atoms.question: Can I get Medicare coverage if I never worked?
atoms.text: Maybe. Citizens or permanent residents age 65 or older, or with a qualifying disability or medical condition, are eligible for Medicare. You can enroll in Medicare Part A at no cost if your spouse (living or deceased, including a divorced spouse) receives or is eligible to receive Social Security or RRB benefits, if you or your spouse worked long enough in a government job through which you paid Medicare taxes, or if you are the dependent parent of a fully insured deceased child.

atoms.title: Medicare for veterans with VA or TRICARE
atoms.question: What if I qualify for veterans' benefits?
atoms.text: If you're a U.S. veteran, you may have other insurance, such as TRICARE or Veterans Affairs (VA) benefits, but you may still want to enroll in a Medicare plan, and the VA recommends it. Care through the VA covers services at VA facilities or others authorized by the VA, while Medicare can cover care at private hospitals and doctors outside the VA system. Having both means you can get care in more places.

atoms.title: Disability and Medicare timing
atoms.question: I'm on disability. When will I be eligible for Medicare?
atoms.text: It depends on your disability. If you have been receiving Social Security Disability Insurance benefits for at least 24 months, you should be eligible for Medicare coverage.

atoms.title: Next steps once you're eligible
atoms.question: I'm eligible for Medicare. What do I do next?
atoms.text: If you first become eligible because you are turning 65, you will have an Initial Enrollment Period (IEP) that begins three months before the month of your 65th birthday and ends three months afterward. During your IEP, you can enroll in Original Medicare (Part A and/or Part B). Then you can choose to enroll in a Medicare Advantage (Part C) or Medicare Part D prescription drug plan, or apply for a Medicare Supplement (Medigap) insurance plan.
